catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress. Primary stress is often realized by a lengthening of the syllable peak of the stressed syllable. Stress is phonemic in Mengen as seen in the minimal pairs in (24-26). 24) a. ['ma.si] 'good, well' b. [ma.'si] 'hole' 25) a. ['ma.ra] 'loose stones on beach' b. [ma.'ra] 'sunrise' 26) a. ['i.lo] 'type of fish' b. [i.'lo] 'type of dance' Examples (27-30) below show phonemic stress in three and four-syllable words. ... 3.5 Stress. While stress is phonemic in Mengen, as shown in 2.3, it is to be noted that there are many words that generally carry stress in certain environments. I state these generalizations here and follow them with pertinent examples and any notable exceptions. 3.5.1 Generalisations in open syllables. new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is phonemic in Mengen, but it has low functional load: 'mara 'loose stones on beach' 'patong 'say' ma'ra 'sunrise' pa'tong 'pile/gather'
new_statements.citation: [Not in the works list; already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass and re-read for context] Madden, Fred. 2001. Mengen Organised Phonology Data. Ukarumpa: SIL. 4 pp. ms. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42370)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 4 pages, header 'Mengen (Poeng) Language [MEE], West Pomio and Central Pomio Census Divisions - East New Britain Province', 'Data checked by: Madden (2001)', footer 'Mengen (Poeng) OPD Printed: August 27, 2004'). extracted text of the PDF gives, exactly as quoted: 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) / Stress is phonemic in Mengen, but it has low functional load: / 'mara 'loose stones on beach' 'patong 'say' / ma'ra 'sunrise' pa'tong 'pile/gather''. The same page continues with phonemic consonant length (osi/ossi, mama/mamma, ona/onna) and vowel lengthening for amplification (bollauu, gaviili), neither tied to stress; the Syllable Patterns and Conventions sections say nothing further abo…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog entry for Mengen has an empty rule; this source supplies the only explicit statement found: stress is phonemic with low functional load, illustrated by initial- vs second-syllable minimal pairs. It is Madden's own OPD, on the same Poeng dialect as the two listed works. Header: 'Mengen (Poeng) Language [MEE], West Pomio and Central Pomio Census Divisions - East New Britain Province'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) in Mengen but distinguishes few words; in the two disyllabic minimal pairs given, stress falls on the first syllable in one member and on the second in the other, so placement is not predictable from the segmental string. No general default position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the same page adds that consonant length is phonemic (osi/ossi, mama/mamma, ona/onna) and that vowel lengthening conveys amplification (bollau 'big' vs bollauu 'very big'), but neither is tied to stress
new_statements.identity_note: All three Madden works describe the Poeng (coastal, Jacquinot Bay) dialect of Mengen [mee]: the OPD is headed 'Mengen (Poeng) Language [MEE]' and the discourse paper states (p. 3, section 1 and fn. 1) 'Ross (1988) places Mengen, or more specifically the Poeng dialect of Mengen upon which this paper is based, under the Proto Mengen branch.. Both Ross and Chowning (1976) refer to the dialect of Mengen spoken along or near the coast of Jacquinot Bay as Poeng', naming the Orford dialect and the Longeinga or Bush Mengen dialect as the other two; fieldwork base Manginuna village since 1990. The dictionary is by the same compiler, same programme.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on the page images we hold of Rath 1993 p. 75 (sec. 2.3) and p. 87 (sec. 3.5-3.5.2); locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1993 dedicated SIL phonology sketch (28 pp) by the primary fieldworker, the only 'phonology' entry for Mengen in Glottolog 5.1 (4 descriptive refs total) and in SIL's own PNG listing; no later grammar, dissertation, or instrumental study located. (3) downloaded now: Madden 2001 OPD p. 3 independently states 'Stress is phonemic in Mengen, but it has low functional load' with the same minimal pairs -- confirms lexical; Müller 1907 Anthropos Lautlehre is silent on stress placement. Remaining unheld items (Rath 1986 unpublished grammar ms; Madden 2006 dictionary) are low priority and unlikely to change the classification.
